Intel (INTC) Faces Lawsuit And AI Selloff As Fair Value Debate Gets Harder

INTC
Trade Intel on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Intel (INTC) is under pressure after a sector-wide selloff in semiconductor and AI stocks coincided with a new class action lawsuit accusing the company of misleading disclosures about its slowing PC business and AI positioning.

The share price has retreated sharply in the past month, with a 30-day share price return of down 39.8% and a 90-day move of down 40.9%, even though Intel's year-to-date share price return is still up 38.3% and the 1-year total shareholder return is 48%. This points to long-term holders still sitting on gains, while recent momentum has clearly faded as legal headlines and a broad AI and semiconductor selloff reset expectations around risk.

Scan how other chipmakers are handling the same AI and PC reset by lining up Intel's slide against 52 AI infrastructure stocks that could be next in line for sharp sentiment swings.

Intel still has scale, technology partnerships and an entrenched PC and data center footprint. After a near 40% slide in 30 days, are you paying for a strong franchise or overpaying for a complicated turnaround?

Most Popular Narrative: 89.1% Undervalued

Against Intel's last close at $54.47, the most followed community narrative pegs fair value at $500.93 per share, a huge gap that frames the lawsuit and price slide in a very different light. According to Suen, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community who authored the narrative, the core of the thesis sits in x86 software lock-in and the foundry footprint in the US.

Compared to ARM, x86 does face an overhead penalty due to hypervisor translation on the assumption that ARM has been natively built. However, the majority of applications are not natively built (aside from webpages), which would mean ARM would suffer a significant emulation penalty in terms of performance. Additionally, even with a natively compiled binary for ARM, x86 could still come out on top due to ARM being less cache efficient, as the same application compiled for ARM generates larger code objects, which could lower cache hit rate (depending on application).

Steve Cohen's Point72 Asset Management filed its third-quarter 13F with the SEC on November 16, reporting about $90.0 billion in holdings at September 30, including options, according to 13f.info. That snapshot predates the Nasdaq Composite's 5.5% drop on November 5, its biggest one-day fall in 19 months, which left the index more than 10% below its October 6 record and confirmed a correction, Reuters reported. Chipmakers led the losses on fears of tougher AI regulation after Democrats won control of the US Congress, so the filing shows how Cohen's fund was positioned before the drop.

Inside Cohen's Latest Filing

The filing shows big changes near the top of the portfolio. Point72 raised its holding in a software giant from 31,522 shares at June 30 to 2,055,578 at September 30, and it roughly tripled its stake in a US chipmaker over the same period, according to its 13F filings. A 13F lists long stock positions and options at quarter-end, so it does not show when Point72 traded, at what price, or any short positions. Point72 also said on May 18 that Cohen remains chairman, CEO and co-chief investment officer, overseeing its day-to-day operations and investment strategies.

Filings like this one show where professional money sat before the drop, and our ranking of the AI stocks that billionaire investors hold in their portfolios looks at another slice of that money.

Hedge Funds Take a Hit

Cohen's fund is not the only one under pressure. Reuters reported on November 6 that JPMorgan estimated global hedge funds lost 3% in October, when the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.6%, its biggest monthly decline in 18 months. Goldman Sachs estimates showed multi-strategy managers, the group Point72 belongs to, fell 1.4% on November 5, and the research firm PivotalPath warned that the 10 largest multi-strategy funds hold increasingly similar positions, so their selling could hit many of the same securities.

The selling returned on November 17, when the S&P 500 fell 1% for a fourth straight loss and the Dow dropped 1.6%, according to the Associated Press. The Federal Reserve's minutes from its October 27-28 meeting, released the next day, showed that almost all participants judged further rate increases would likely be appropriate. Nasdaq futures rose nearly 2% on November 19 after a record-size AI developer public offering priced above its marketed range, Reuters reported, though LSEG data cited by Reuters show traders see a near-certainty of a quarter-point hike in December. That is the backdrop for the stocks below, which sit among Point72's largest common stock positions and also meet our screening criteria. Nvidia Now Has 41% of Its Stock Portfolio in SpaceX. Here's What That Means for Nvidia Shareholders ©RiverNorthPhotography from Getty Images Signature metamorworks from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Nvidia's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30 shows SpaceX as its largest holding, at 41% of its US stocks, just ahead of Intel.

For Nvidia shareholders, the stake is small: the whole $48.33 billion portfolio is worth less than the $65.3 billion of net income Nvidia earned in its latest quarter.

SpaceX matters more to Nvidia as a customer. It's building out Nvidia's newest systems while spending far more cash than its business brings in.

SpaceX's earnings estimates have risen while its stock fell 16% since Sept. 30, so the numbers back Nvidia's stake. How SpaceX pays for its buildout is the thing to watch.

Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) has a new biggest holding, and it's also one of Nvidia's customers: SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ).

Nvidia's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 16, shows 130.47 million SpaceX shares worth $19.68 billion. That's 40.7% of the $48.33 billion of US-listed stocks the filing holds.

SpaceX passed Intel by a nose

That puts SpaceX just ahead of Intel (INTC:NASDAQ), Nvidia's largest holding the quarter before, at 40.1%. Nvidia held 6% more SpaceX shares at Sept. 30 than at June 30. It held about a quarter fewer Intel shares: 161.08 million, down from 214.8 million.

The gap has only grown since. SpaceX is down 16% from its Sept. 30 price, while Intel is down 55%, with a $1.6 billion guidance miss along the way. Even so, the Intel shares Nvidia still holds cost it $23.28 each in 2025, so it's sitting on a big gain at Intel's last close of $54.47.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Nvidia, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Nvidia's Analyst Ratings

The stake is small next to Nvidia's profits

For Nvidia shareholders, the 41% sounds bigger than it is. Nvidia's whole 13F portfolio is worth $48.33 billion at quarter-end prices. That's less than the $65.3 billion of GAAP net income Nvidia earned in the single quarter ended Oct. 25. It also returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in buybacks and dividends that quarter. And since a 13F covers only US-listed stocks, Nvidia's private stakes aren't in it.

The drop since Sept. 30 will show up in Nvidia's GAAP earnings, which include the gains and losses on its stakes. Its non-GAAP earnings leave them out. So a weaker SpaceX and Intel can drag on GAAP EPS for a quarter while the chip business carries on.

One company drawing particular attention is the chipmaker Intel (INTC), which has seen mixed moves among major hedge funds and institutional investors. According to the latest reports, Nvidia (NVDA) remained Intel's largest institutional holder in the latest quarter, despite cutting its position by 25% to 161.08 million shares.

Meanwhile, several prominent investors, including Soros Fund, Tiger Capital, and Maverick Capital, increased their holdings, while Lone Pine and Discovery Capital initiated new positions. SoftBank (SFTBY) also maintained its substantial 86.96 million-share stake.

But what do these moves mean for Intel, and should investors view them as a positive sign for the stock? Let's try to figure it out.

Intel Stock's Rally Has Unravelled

The performance of Intel stock has been outstanding in the past two years, rising by over 130%. But it's up about 57% from the start of the year—and down about 60% from the June 30 high of $142.35.

The selloff came after data from Intel on Oct. 29 that revealed its earnings fell short of expectations. The Q3 results came in above expectations, but Q4 was slightly disappointing relative to Wall Street expectations. Intel predicted revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion and an adjusted EPS of $0.25, mostly short of estimates of $17.1 billion and $0.43.

Intel is constrained in its ability to deliver more data center CPUs in part because of declining sales of PCs and a shortage of parts like memory. A fatal explosion at its Fab 28 facility in Israel has put further pressure on the supply of its server products. In some quarters, there's lower demand, and in others, Intel is having trouble meeting higher demand.

ASE Technology Holding ASX is benefiting from accelerating demand for leading-edge advanced packaging (LEAP) services, driven by increasing artificial intelligence infrastructure investments and growing semiconductor complexity. In the third quarter of 2026, consolidated revenues surged 44.8% year over year to a record NT$244.2 billion, benefiting from faster-than-expected installations of high-demand LEAP capacity.

Strong LEAP demand supported assembly and testing (ATM) revenues, which increased 51% year over year to a record NT$151.5 billion. Computing applications, which account for the majority of LEAP services, represented 34% of ATM revenues compared with 25% in the year-ago quarter. Increasing LEAP contributions and higher capacity utilization also helped ATM gross margin expand 800 basis points year over year to 30.6%.

Reflecting robust customer demand, ASE Technology raised its 2026 LEAP revenue projection from $3.7 billion to more than $4 billion and expects revenues to double in 2027. Full-process packaging revenues are projected to increase from $300 million in 2026 to more than $1 billion in 2027, while co-packaged optics is expected to contribute more than $500 million to LEAP revenues next year.

To capitalize on demand exceeding available capacity, ASX raised its 2026 capital expenditure guidance to $11.5 billion. More than half of its 22 ongoing building projects in Taiwan are expected to start supporting revenues through 2027.

Hence, accelerating LEAP demand, expanding advanced packaging capabilities and aggressive capacity investments position ASE Technology to sustain strong revenue growth through 2027 and beyond. Reflecting these favorable trends, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for 2027 revenues is pegged at 26.56%.

How Are ASX's Competitors Positioned?

Amkor Technology AMKR is benefiting from growing demand for advanced semiconductor packaging and testing solutions across AI and high-performance computing applications. In the third quarter of 2026, Amkor Technology achieved record computing revenues, supported by increasing adoption of high-density fan-out packaging. Expanding 2.5D packaging programs, strengthening hyperscaler engagements and investments in its Arizona manufacturing facility are expected to enhance Amkor Technology's competitive positioning against ASX.

Intel Corporation INTC is strengthening its presence in advanced semiconductor packaging through its EMIB, EMIB-T and Foveros technologies, addressing growing demand for high-performance AI chips. In the third quarter of 2026, Intel reported significant external customer traction for its advanced packaging technologies. Expanding manufacturing capacity in New Mexico and Malaysia to support customer demand in 2027 is expected to strengthen Intel's competitive position against ASE Technology.

Tech stocks stalled Wednesday as the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.6% and Nvidia (NVDA) lost 4%. AI spending doubts and fresh inflation data cut short Monday's rebound.

Still, the Nasdaq recovered from steeper intraday losses, even as chip stocks closed lower. That leaves holders of Nvidia, Micron Technology (MU), and Oracle (ORCL) exposed when markets reopen Friday for a shortened session.

Why Did the Tech Stocks Rebound Fade So Fast?

Nvidia posted one of its best sessions on record Monday. Jensen Huang had just returned as CEO after resigning on Nov. 12.

However, Nvidia has since slid, including 4% Wednesday, while Micron lost 4% and Oracle fell over 5%.

Nvidia has lost much of its 2026 gains. Source: Trading View

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Marvell Technology (MRVL), and Intel (INTC) edged lower. Meanwhile, the VanEck Semiconductor exchange-traded fund (ETF), ticker SMH, shed 1%.

The weakness had already spread to Asia. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fell more than 7% in an Asian chip sell-off earlier Wednesday.

Is This Panic or a Macro Warning?

Core Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation, which excludes food and energy, rose 3.3% from a year earlier in October.

Economists had forecast 3.2%, according to Morningstar. As a result, worries grew that higher interest rates would weigh on growth stocks.

Venu Krishna, head of U.S. equity strategy at Barclays, offered a blunt read on CNBC.

"We just feel that this is panic right now."

Krishna added.

"What the market is telling you is that the AI growth narrative has hit a wall and given the centrality of that theme at the economic level, the market is expecting some sort of a macro shock."

In contrast, Anthropic (ANT), the maker of the Claude AI model, bucked the trend. Its shares gained more than 4% after slipping below the $83 initial public offering (IPO) price.

Elsewhere, Michael Burry disclosed a temporary bullish shift Wednesday after the Nasdaq 100 briefly fell 20% below its record.

Markets reopen Friday for a shortened session. The AI trade may hinge on whether rate fears ease and whether AI spending begins to pay off.
